                                                        Abstract
     We revisit Blackwell’s celebrated approachability problem which considers a repeated vector-
     valued game between a player and an adversary. Motivated by settings in which the action set
     of the player or adversary (or both) is difficult to optimize over, for instance when it corresponds to
     the set of all possible solutions to some NP-Hard optimization problem, we ask what can the player
     guarantee efficiently, when only having access to these sets via approximation algorithms with ra-

     that he does not prefer a vector-valued loss `1 over `2 if `2 ≤ `1 , we establish that given a Blackwell

1. Introduction
In his seminal paper from the 1950s, Blackwell presented his celebrated approachability problem
and theorem (Blackwell, 1956). Blackwell considered repeated vector-valued games in which on
each iteration t, the first player, which we shall simply refer to as the player, picks an action xt from
a fixed compact and convex set X , which is then followed by the second player, which we shall refer
to as the adversary, choosing his action yt from another fixed compact and convex set Y, and then,
a corresponding vector-valued loss `(xt , yt ) is revealed, where we shall assume throughout that ` is
a fixed and known bi-linear function. The game then continues to the next round. Focusing on the
view-point of the player, his goal in this game is to obtain average (over time) loss, whose distance
(say in Euclidean norm) to some fixed and pre-specified convex and closed target set S, goes to zero
as the length of the game goes to infinity, no matter how the adversary plays. In case this goal is
feasible, the target set S is said to be approachable. Blackwell gave both a characterization when a
set S is approachable, and an algorithm for choosing the actions of the player so that approachability
is indeed obtained.
     The literature on approachability is vast and we do not presume to appropriately survey it here.
Instead we refer the interested reader to (Maschler et al., 2020; Perchet, 2014; Cesa-Bianchi and
Lugosi, 2006) and references therein.
     Algorithms for choosing the player’s actions so that approachability to the target set is guaran-
teed (when possible), naturally require, as a sub-procedure, to solve certain optimization problems
with respect to the actions sets of the player and the adversary (and also the target set S). In this
work however, we are interested in the case in which such optimizations may be computationally-
infeasible. For instance, when one of these sets, X or Y (or both), corresponds to the set of all

all such solutions, to include mixed-actions). As an example, we can think that the action the player
needs to take on each round of the game is to select a vertex cover or a Hamiltonian cycle in some
fixed combinatorial graph, or that the adversary’s action corresponds to choosing a cut in some fixed
combinatorial graph (see a more detailed example in the sequel). In such a case, while the Blackwell
instance might be approachable, it might not be efficiently approachable, since no polynomial-time
algorithm that can guarantee approachability is known (or even widely expected to exist). Instead,
in such a case it is natural to assume that the action sets (those for which optimization is difficult)
are accessible through a computationally-efficient approximation algorithm (approximation oracle
henceforth) with some ratio α > 0. If α > 1, then for any non-negative linear objective, the oracle
returns a point in the action set whose value is at most α times that of the action with minimal value;
if α < 1, the oracle returns a point in the action set whose value is at least α times that of the action
with maximal value. The question is then, what can the player guarantee (w.r.t. his average loss)
using only a polynomial (in the natural parameters of the problem) number of calls to these oracles
(and additional polynomial running time).

    Our approach builds heavily on several techniques from online convex optimization (OCO)
(Hazan, 2019). First, we use the approach introduced in (Abernethy et al., 2011) and later refined
in (Shimkin, 2016), to reduce approachability to online convex optimization over the Euclidean unit
ball. This approach however requires access to what is referred to as an halfspace oracle (Aber-
nethy et al., 2011), which in principle could be implemented by solving a saddle-point optimization
problem w.r.t. the action sets X , Y, however cannot be efficiently implemented in our setting. In-
stead, we introduce what we refer to as an infeasible saddle-point oracle, which in a sense, solves
these problems w.r.t. a modified Blackwell instance, while providing guarantees that are feasible
w.r.t. the original instance. Implementing these new oracles also uses machinery from OCO to
implement primal-dual methods (which is a well-studied technique, see for instance (Hazan, 2006))
in a novel way that can solve these infeasible saddle-point problems via access to approximation
oracles.
    Finally, our work is related, and in fact very much inspired by the problem of online linear
optimization with approximation algorithms, studied in (Kakade et al., 2007) and later revisited in
(Garber, 2017) and (Hazan et al., 2018). In this line of work, it is shown how to turn an approxi-
mation oracle with ratio α for an offline linear optimization problem, into an efficient algorithm for
the corresponding online linear optimization problem with approximately the same approximation
guarantee, i.e., to guarantee sub-linear regret w.r.t. α times the cumulative loss/payoff of the best ac-
tion in hindsight. While, to the best of our understanding, these algorithms cannot be applied in our
approachability setting, some techniques introduced in (Kakade et al., 2007), such as the extended
approximation oracle and the use of the Frank-Wolfe technique for computing so-called infeasible
projections, are also used as building blocks in the construction of our algorithms.
